Here M can be taken as 12,500 tons per square inch for gun steel. In the example already calculated the shrinkage between the jacket and barrel is 0·009 in.

{{block center|<math>\text{S} = \frac{2\times 4\cdot 1}{12,500}\left[6\cdot 43 + 11\cdot 25 + \frac{(4\cdot 1)^2 - (2\cdot 5)^2}{(4\cdot 1)^2 + (2\cdot 5)^2}(-11\cdot 25 + 3\cdot 4)\right]</math>}}

''Wire guns.''—In that portion of the gun in which wire is used in the construction, exactly the same principles are involved. It may be assumed that the tube on which the wire is wound is so large, in comparison to the thickness of the wire, that the compression of the concave surface of the wire and the extension of its convex surface may be neglected without sensible error.

The greatest advantage is obtained from the wire coils when in the Firing Stress the tension T is uniform throughout the thickness of the wiring. The Firing Stress T in the wire may be as low as 25 tons per square inch and as high as 50 tons, but as the yielding strength of the wire is never less than 80 tons per square inch nor its breaking strength less than 90 tons, there is still an ample margin especially when it is remembered that the factor of safety is included in the calculation.

If the wire is wound direct on to the barrel and is covered by a jacket, <math>r_0</math>, <math>r_1</math> being the radii in inches of the barrel, <math>r_1</math>, <math>r_2</math> the radii of the internal and external layers of wire, and <math>r_2</math>, <math>r_3</math> the radii of the jacket; then for the Firing Stress in the wire

{{block center|<math>\text{T}(r_2 - r) = \text{P}r - \text{P}_2r_2</math> (9),}}

or

{{block center|<math>\text{T}(r - r_1) = \text{P}_1r_1 - \text{P}r</math> (10).}}

By combining these the gunmakers' formula for the wire is obtained {{block center|<math>\text{P}_1 = \frac{r_2 - r_1}{r_1}(\text{T} + \text{P}_2) + \text{P}_2</math> (10''a'').}}

As <math>\text{T}</math> is to be uniform, when the gun is fired, the Initial Tensions of the wire are arranged accordingly, and the tensions at which the wire must be wound on to the guns have now to be determined.

Let <math>\theta</math> = the winding tension at radius <math>r</math> in.

<math>(t)</math> = the initial tension at radius <math>r</math> in.

<math>(p)</math> = the radial pressure between any two layers of wire at radius <math>r</math> in.

It is assumed that <math>\text{M}</math> is uniform for the gun steel and wire. Then
{{block center|<math>\theta = (t) + (p)\frac{r^2 + r_0^2}{r^2 - r_0^2}</math> (11),}}
where
{{block center|<math>(t) = \text{T} - \text{P}_0\frac{r_0^2}{r^2}\,\frac{r_2^2 + r^2}{r_2^2 - r_0^2}</math> (12),}}
and
{{block center|<math>(p) = \text{P} - \text{P}_0\frac{r_0^2}{r^2}\,\frac{r_2^2 - r^2}{r_2^2 - r_0^2}</math> (13).}}

By means of these two equations and (9) the expression (11) becomes
{{block center|<math>\theta = \frac{\text{E}}{r} + \frac{\text{F}}{r - r_0} + \frac{\text{G}}{r + r_0}</math> (14),}}
where
{{block center|<math>\text{E} = -(\text{T} + \text{P}_2)r_2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\text{F} = (\text{T} + \text{P}_2)r_2 - (\text{T} + \text{P}_0)r_0</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\text{G} = (\text{T} + \text{P}_2)r_2 + (\text{T} + \text{P}_0)r_0</math>.}}

To compare with the previous example, the stress for a 4·7-in. Q.F. wire gun will be calculated. This consists of a barrel, intermediate layer of wire and jacket.

Here <math>r_0 = 2\cdot 5</math>; <math>r_1 = 3\cdot 75</math>; <math>r_2 = 5\cdot 5</math>; <math>r_3 = 7\cdot 5</math> inches; the firing tension <math>\text{T}_1</math> to <math>\text{T}'_2</math> of the wire = 25 tons per square inch, suppose.

Take <math>\text{P}_0 = 21</math> tons per square inch and consider that the jacket fits tightly over the wire, but has no shrinkage. Then for the ''Firing Stress'', from (2), <math>\text{P}_2 = 2\cdot 25</math> tons, and from (9) and (10), <math>\text{T}_1(r_2 - r_1) = \text{P}_1r_1 - \text{P}_2r_2</math>
{{block center|<math>\text{P}_1 = 14\cdot 97, \text{ say } 15 \text{ tons}</math>,}}
from (4) we can obtain <math>\text{T}_0</math> and <math>\text{T}_2</math> since <math>\text{P}_0</math>, <math>\text{P}_1</math> and <math>\text{P}_2</math> are known; from (3) <math>\text{T}_0 = 0\cdot 6</math> tons. <math>\text{T}_2 = 7\cdot 5</math> tons.
{{block center|<math>\text{T}'_2 = -5\cdot 4 \text{ tons (a compression)}</math>,}}
and
{{block center|<math>\text{T}_3 = 5\cdot 25 \text{ tons}</math>.}}

The ''Powder Stress'' is obtained in the same way as in the previous example, so also is the ''Initial Stress''; therefore we may tabulate as follows:— {{block center|<math>\begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc}

\text{Radius.} & \text{Firing Stress.} & \text{Powder Stress.} & \text{Initial Stress.} & \text{Firing Stress.} & \text{Powder Stress.} & \text{Initial Stress.} \\
\hline

\end{array}</math>}}

As the wire is wound on, the pressure of the external layers will compress those on the interior, thus producing an extension in the wire which is equivalent to a reduction in the winding tension <math>\theta</math> of the particular layer at radius <math>r</math> considered. If <math>\tau</math> represents this reduction then
{{block center|<math>\theta = (t) - \tau,</math>}}
where
{{block center|<math>\tau = -\frac{r^2 + r_0^2}{r^2 - r_0^2}(p)</math>}}

At the interior layer of wire <math>\tau</math> is the initial stress on the exterior of the barrel and the winding tension must commence at
{{block center|<math>\theta = 11\cdot875 + 18\cdot525 = 30\cdot4</math> tons per square inch.}}

As the jacket is supposed to have no shrinkage <math>\text{T} = 0</math> and consequently
{{block center|<math>\theta = (t) = 17\cdot5</math> tons per square inch.}}

These winding tensions can be found directly from formula (14) and then
{{block center|<math>\text{E} = -149\cdot875;\ \text{F} = 34\cdot875;\ \text{G} = 264\cdot875.</math>}}

Sir G. Greenhill has put these formulas, both for the built-up and wire-wound guns, into an extremely neat and practical geometrical form, which can be used instead of the arithmetical processes; for these see ''Text-Book of Gunnery'', ''Treatise of Service Ordnance'', 1893, and ''Journal of the United States Artillery'', vol. iv.

''Longitudinal stress.'' The longitudinal strength of the gun is very important especially at the breech end; along the forward portion of the gun the thickness of the barrel and the interlocking of the covering hoops provide ample strength, but at the breech special provision must be made. It is usual to provide for this by means of a strong breech piece or jacket in small guns or by both combined in large ones. Its amount is easily calculated on the hypothesis that the stress is uniformly distributed throughout the thickness of the breech piece, or jacket, or of both. If <math>r_0</math> is the largest radius of the gun chamber, <math>r_{01}</math> the radius of the obturator seating, <math>r_1</math> the external radius of the barrel, and <math>\text{P}_0</math> the maximum powder pressure, then, with the usual form of chamber adopted with guns fitted with obturation other than cartridge cases, there will be a longitudinal stress on the barrel at the breech end of the chamber due to the action of the pressure <math>\text{P}_0</math> on the rear slope of the chamber, of
{{block center|<math>\frac{\pi}{4}(r_0^2 - r_{01}^2)\text{P}_0 \text{ tons}</math>}}
this is resisted by the barrel of section <math>\frac{\pi}{4}(r_1^2 - r_0^2)</math> so that the resistance
{{block center|<math>\text{R} = \frac{r_0^2 - r_{01}^2}{r_1^2 - r_0^2}\text{P}_0 \text{ tons}.</math>}}

This portion of the longitudinal stress is not of great importance as the breech end of the barrel is supported in all modern designs by the breech bush. In Q.F. guns, ''i.e.'' those firing cartridge cases, the breech end of the chamber has the largest diameter, and <math>r_0 = r_{01}</math> so that there is no longitudinal stress on the chamber part of the barrel.

For the breech piece or outer tube of radii <math>r_1</math> and <math>r_2</math>, the resistance
{{block center|<math>\text{R} = \frac{r_{01}^2}{r_2^2 - r_1^2}\text{P}_0 \text{ tons for B.L. guns} = \frac{r_0^2}{r_2^2 - r_1^2}\text{P}_0</math> tons in Q.F. guns.}}

If the longitudinal stress is taken by a jacket only, the resistance is found in the same way.

Generally for ordinary gun steel, the longitudinal stress on the material is always kept below 10 tons per square inch or 13 tons for nickel steel; but even with these low figures there is also included a factor of safety of 1·5 to 2. In large guns it is best to consider the jacket as an auxiliary aid only to longitudinal resistance, as, owing to the necessary connexions between it and the breech bush and its distance from the centre of pressure, there is a possibility that it may not be taking its proportionate share of the stress.
